newsitem.title: RUSSIA: From sea to sea, Russians march in protest.
newsitem.headline: From sea to sea, Russians march in protest.

text.p: From the Pacific Ocean to the Baltic Sea, hundreds of thousands of Russians vented pent-up anger on the streets on Thursday, flying the red flag of communism and marching to brass bands.

"This march is going from Vladivostok to Kaliningrad and no one can stop it," Communist party leader Gennady Zyuganov told reporters, referring to the Pacific and Baltic ports. He was taking part in the biggest rally in Moscow.
But turnout was well below the millions forecast by trade unions. There were no reports of violence despite opposition warnings Russia was on the verge of Balkan-style anarchy.

The mood across the world's biggest country was a mixture of irritation at not being paid for months combined with the apparently bottomless patience and resignation of a population of 150 million that history has inured to hardship.
"We want change," said one demonstrating worker in the Siberian industrial and high-technology centre of Novosibirsk. "But we don't really expect it."

Vladivostok, 7,000 km (4,500 miles) east of Moscow, took on a festive air reminiscent of Soviet-era May Day parades. Streets were blocked off but the police presence was minimal. Bands played and a crowd of at least 15,000 sang socialist songs.
Local energy companies cut off supplies from clients who had not paid their bills -- part of a web of debt which has ensnared the whole economy but is particulary acute in the Far East.
"First wages, then taxes!" demanded a banner above a gathering of 1,000 in the centre of Magadan, a city synonomous with some of the most brutal Soviet-era GULag labour camps.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's new government says workers are owed more than 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back pay but says it must raise tax revenues if they are to get it.

In the coalfields of southern Siberia, where deputy premier Anatoly Chubais flew last weekend with millions of dollars for wages and a promise to put things right, the once militant miners staged rallies but mostly followed union calls to avoid strike action or calling for the government to resign.
In Yekaterinburg, industrial heart of the Ural mountains and President Boris Yeltsin's hometown, they were less restrained.
"Chubais Out!" was one of the more printable slogans.
The central government representative to the Yekaterinburg region was jeered and the crowds called for Yeltsin to resign.
Near the president's rural birthplace, several hundred angry workers blocked the main road to Siberia for two hours.

In the agricultural and communist Red Belt of southern Russia, thousands heeded the call for "comrades" to take to the streets of Krasnodar. But trade union leaders were left making limp excuses for a less than overwhelming turnout. "Krasnodar doesn't have the same big squares as in Moscow," said one.

In St Petersburg, cradle of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, about 40,000 converged on the historic square in front of the tsars' Winter Palace. But after hours marching in a snowstorm, many drifted away before the speakers even got warmed up.
Russia's second city is traditionally its most liberal but many skilled defence industry technicians and academic experts are among the hardest hit by the economic crisis.
One man carried a skeleton bearing the slogan: "This used to be a biology teacher."

Few expect rapid change. The young, liberal-minded new government is committed to reforms but needs time. And, in any case, five years of commitment to reform has so far failed to provide the bulk of the population with much comfort.

Despite the slogans and the anger, a deeply Russian fatalism was visible across the country, among the silent majority who took no part and among the marchers too: "We are Russians," proclaimed one banner in Novosibirsk. "God is with Us."
